metadata.title: Measuring skill gaps in firms: the PIAAC Employer Module (EN)
metadata.venue: OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This document is a technical description of the OECD PIAAC Employer Module rather than an empirical analysis of student-level outcomes. It therefore does not report a specific analytic sample, nor does it specify whether complex survey weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were applied in estimation. For any subsequent empirical use of PIAAC Employer Module data, analysts should consult the PIAAC technical documentation for the recommended sampling/estimation weights and variance estimation approach, and apply them to account for the survey’s complex design. Because no model-based results are presented here, weighting variables (if any) are not identifiable from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided text describes the conceptual development and technical specifications of the PIAAC Employer Module, but it does not report any empirical estimation results that would require plausible values (PVs) or a documented PV strategy. In addition, the excerpt does not specify any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., imputation or deletion rules), so the missing-data strategy cannot be extracted from the available content. This is best treated as a reporting gap for missing-data handling details in the excerpt, not as evidence that a particular method was or was not used.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No analytic sample, country coverage, or inclusion/exclusion rules are reported in the provided excerpt. The document instead outlines the Employer Module’s purpose and technical specifications (questionnaire development, units of observation/coverage, administration mode, and data cleaning/validation requirements).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper introduces the PIAAC Employer Module as a new survey instrument intended to measure workplace skill gaps—imbalances between the supply and demand for skills—and to link these gaps to firms’ business strategy and hiring, training, and human resource practices. The document focuses on how the module complements worker-level information from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills, and it details key technical features such as questionnaire conceptual development, units of observation and coverage, mode of administration, and requirements for data cleaning and validation. No empirical model estimates, predictive performance metrics, or benchmark comparisons are reported in the provided text. As a result, the contribution is primarily methodological and design-oriented: it establishes what data will be collected and how it should be prepared for future analyses of skill gaps in firms.
